opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of those claims come from looking at the wrong measurements. If your yardstick is a benchmark that's already ninety-something percent saturated, then of course the line looks flat. There's no headroom left to show progress. That says more about the eval than about the model.

When we build evaluations that are harder and closer to real work, the picture looks very different. These are tasks where an expert in law, finance, nursing, or engineering sits down and produces an actual deliverable. On those, we keep seeing meaningful jumps from one generation to the next. Models are getting better at longer tasks, at following through on multi-step work, and at producing something a professional would actually use rather than something that just looks plausible.

Part of it is also perception. Once a capability arrives, people adjust to it really quickly. Something that felt like magic a year ago now feels like table stakes, so each new improvement can feel incremental even when it's substantial. And a lot of the recent gains are in areas that are harder to notice in a casual chat, like reliability, reasoning over long contexts, and agentic tasks.

So my view is that the "wall" is often a measurement problem. That's why I think it's so important to keep building evals grounded in real-world value. They tell us honestly where models are improving, and also where they still fall short, because there are definitely still gaps. But "there's more to do" is very different from "progress has stopped."

r001.rationale: The response attributes expectations of continued improvement to better evaluations and observed gains, but does not cite OpenAI’s research roadmap.

r002.rationale: It says people quickly adjust to new capabilities and that progress can feel incremental, but does not judge public expectations of AI models to be too low.

fable-5.1.text:
I honestly think those claims are a little bit funny, because every few months somebody declares a wall, and then a few months later the models are doing things people were confidently saying they couldn't do. I spend a lot of my time working on evaluations, and from where I sit, the evidence points the other way. The benchmarks that were supposed to be hard are saturating faster than we can build new ones. That's actually one of our biggest problems right now, not the models stalling, but keeping measurement ahead of capability.

I think part of what's going on is that progress has shifted in character. In the early scaling era, you could see improvement very visibly in things like fluency or basic reasoning, and that was easy for everyone to feel. Now a lot of the gains show up in domains where most people can't personally judge the output. If a model goes from solving ten percent of expert-level research math problems to forty percent, that's an enormous jump, but it doesn't change the experience of asking it for a recipe. So people's intuitions lag the actual frontier.

The other thing is that the levers have multiplied. It's not just pretraining scale anymore. Reasoning, test-time compute, better post-training, tool use, long-horizon agentic work, all of these are compounding on each other. When one axis slows, another one is usually just getting started. So when I hear "the wall," I mostly hear someone looking at one axis.

That said, I'd push back on my own side too. We should be humble about predicting the exact pace. What I'd rather do than argue about walls is build evaluations that are genuinely hard, grounded in real-world expert tasks, and then just let the data speak. So far, every time we've done that, the models have kept climbing.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites benchmark saturation and multiple capability levers, but does not cite OpenAI’s research roadmap.

r002.rationale: The candidate says people’s intuitions lag the frontier, indicating public expectations are too low relative to model progress.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we’ve hit a wall. But I do think progress is becoming harder to capture with a single benchmark or a single model release. The question is: Can these systems solve more difficult problems, and can they do that reliably enough to be useful?

You can have a model that does something impressive once, but still needs a lot of help to complete a task consistently. Closing that gap is meaningful progress. So I’d be cautious about both extremes—saying progress has stopped, or assuming every limitation will disappear with the next model. We should look at what the systems can actually do and where they still fail.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that progress has not stopped, but does not cite OpenAI’s research roadmap as a reason to expect continued improvement.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not judge public expectations to be too low; it cautions against both overly pessimistic and overly optimistic assumptions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “hit a wall” is too strong. Progress isn’t one-dimensional: there’s how capable the underlying model is, but also how reliably it can use tools, work through a problem, and carry a task to completion. Those can improve at different rates.

The question I’d ask is: can the system do something useful today that it couldn’t do before? And can it do it consistently? A model getting a problem right once is very different from someone being able to depend on it in their work. There’s still a lot of room to improve that reliability, and I wouldn’t equate uneven progress with a fundamental ceiling.

r001.rationale: The response expects continued improvement based on reliability and tool use, but does not cite OpenAI’s research roadmap.

r002.rationale: The response says progress has room to improve, but does not judge public expectations of AI models to be too low.
